California.text: The name likely comes from a mythical island in a 1510 story, where warrior women bred griffins for war.
California.evidence: The name is most likely derived from the mythical island of California in the fictional story of Queen Calafia, as recorded in a 1510 work The Adventures of Esplandián by Garci Rodríguez de Montalvo. Queen Calafia's kingdom was said to be a remote land rich in gold and pearls, inhabited by beautiful dark-skinned women who wore gold armor and lived like Amazons, and bred griffins for war.

Texas.text: Under Spanish rule in the 1700s, the area was known as the New Philippines.
Texas.evidence: During Spanish colonial rule, in the 18th century, the area was known as Nuevas Filipinas ('New Philippines') and Nuevo Reino de Filipinas ('New Kingdom of the Philippines')

Florida.text: Ponce de León's search for the Fountain of Youth is a myth that only appeared long after his death.
Florida.evidence: The first recorded European explorers to reach Florida were Spaniards led by Juan Ponce de León, who sighted the peninsula on April 2, 1513, and came ashore the next day to seek information and take possession of this new land. ... The story that he was searching for the Fountain of Youth is apocryphal and appeared only long after his death.

New York.text: The Dutch retook New York City in 1673 and renamed it New Orange, then handed it back a year later.
New York.evidence: The city of New York was recaptured by the Dutch in 1673 during the Third Anglo-Dutch War (1672–1674) and renamed New Orange. It was returned to the English under the terms of the Treaty of Westminster a year later.

Pennsylvania.text: William Penn wanted to call it New Wales, and the name Pennsylvania embarrassed him: it sounded like vanity.
Pennsylvania.evidence: Penn proposed that the land be called New Wales, but there were objections to that name, so he recommended Sylvania (from the Latin silva: "forest, woods"). The King named it Pennsylvania (literally "Penn's Woods") in honor of Admiral Penn. The younger Penn was embarrassed at this name, fearing that people would think he had named it after himself, but King Charles would not rename the grant.

Illinois.text: The first plan left it no Lake Michigan shore; its delegate lobbied the border north and won it the Chicago River.
Illinois.evidence: Such a boundary would have left Illinois with no shoreline on Lake Michigan at all. ... However, the Illinois delegate, Nathaniel Pope, wanted more, and lobbied to have the boundary moved further north. ... More importantly, it added nearly 50 miles of Lake Michigan shoreline and the Chicago River.

Ohio.text: Congress forgot to formally admit it as a state; the slip was found in 1953 and fixed retroactively.
Ohio.evidence: Congress, however, did not formally admit Ohio as the 17th state. After the oversight was discovered in 1953 during preparations for Ohio's sesquicentennial, Congressman George H. Bender introduced legislation retroactively admitting Ohio effective March 1, 1803, the date the Ohio General Assembly first convened.

Georgia.text: In 1958 a nuclear bomb was lost off Tybee Island; officials thought it lay buried in silt in Wassaw Sound.
Georgia.evidence: On February 5, 1958, during a training mission flown by a B-47, a Mark 15 nuclear bomb, also known as the Tybee Bomb, was lost off the coast of Tybee Island near Savannah. The bomb was thought by the Department of Energy to lie buried in silt at the bottom of Wassaw Sound.

North Carolina.text: Loyalists called Mecklenburg County "a hornet's nest" of radicals, which later gave Charlotte's NBA team its name.
North Carolina.evidence: British loyalists dubbed the Mecklenburg County area to be 'a hornet's nest' of radicals, birthing the name of the future Charlotte NBA team.

Michigan.text: It lost the Toledo War, a border fight with Ohio, and got the western Upper Peninsula as a concession.
Michigan.evidence: Congressional recognition was delayed pending resolution of a boundary dispute with Ohio known as the Toledo War. Congress awarded the "Toledo Strip" to Ohio. Michigan received the western part of the Upper Peninsula as a concession and formally entered the Union as a free state on January 26, 1837.
